items.question: Is the nanosatellite/CubeSat mission context and lifecycle stage described clearly enough to interpret applicability?
items.rationale: The New Space/small-satellite context and lifecycle layers are clear, but the demonstration mission is not named or characterized in technical detail.

items.question: Are the MBSE method, language, toolchain, model artifacts, and system boundary described clearly enough to support replication or comparison?
items.rationale: The method, toolchain, layers, artifacts, and automation architecture are sufficiently described for comparison and partial replication, though not accompanied by released code.

Section III.C: 'Python scripts are used to to read and write from/to the Capella model.'

items.question: Are claimed outcomes explicitly linked to MBSE artifacts, MBSE activities, or model-enabled process changes rather than asserted generically?
items.rationale: Most benefits are tied to functional libraries, Capella elements, object-oriented grouping, automated generation, and digital-thread data flow.
evidence: Abstract: 'An automated framework was developed to support fast, consistent deployment of satellite digital models across missions'.
Section III.B: 'automating a modular functional design enables standardized digital replicability of the logical architecture and traceability of the model'.
Section IV: 'automated generation of model elements via extended API interfaces.'

items.question: Is evidence provided for claimed outcomes, such as metrics, baseline comparison, case-study results, executable simulation results, model checks, stakeholder evaluation, reuse evidence, integration/test results, or flight/operational data?
items.rationale: A pilot implementation, manual inspection, and Capella model validation provide some evidence, but the paper gives no metrics, comparator, stakeholder evaluation, flight data, or integration-test results.
evidence: Section IV: 'A pilot implementation of the proposed modeling approach was conducted in collaboration with Kongsberg NanoAvionics'.
Section IV: 'manual inspection of the resulting model... and through Capella's built-in model validation tools.'
No quantitative deployment-time, defect-reduction, or reuse metrics are reported.

items.question: Are requirements, verification, validation, design decisions, or lifecycle gates traced to model artifacts when such traceability is central to the paper?
items.rationale: The paper defines and claims traceability across capabilities, functions, logical components, and physical architecture, but it does not show concrete requirement-to-test traces or a trace matrix from the pilot.
evidence: Section II.B: 'MBSE ensures traceability across all system elements'.
Section III.B: 'This approach strengthens traceability between stakeholder needs and system functionality'.
Section III.D: 'preserving traceability to earlier design decisions.'

items.question: Are model availability, open-source assets, reusable packages, data exchange mechanisms, or sufficient implementation details reported to assess reproducibility and toolchain continuity?
items.rationale: The paper reports data exchange formats, APIs, and architecture, but does not report availability of the generated model, scripts, or functional libraries.

Section V: 'Capella does not natively support code-model parallelism'.

quality_checklist.overall_rationale: The paper gives a credible and detailed MBSE automation concept with a pilot implementation and explicit limitations, but evidence is mostly qualitative and system-level; no open artifacts, quantitative comparator, or EPS-specific verification case is provided.

RQ1.rationale: The paper substantially addresses general New Space/small-satellite platform modeling with object-oriented functional groups and automation, but EPS modeling and minimal behavioral knowledge are only indirectly addressed through generic power examples and abstract functional libraries.

RQ2.rationale: It claims reliability-related standardization, replicability, reuse, and integration benefits for satellite platform MBSE, but not as outcomes of EPS-specific modeling.

RQ3.rationale: It describes pre-physical structural and semantic validation of generated Capella models, but not EPS-specific verification procedures or requirements/test integration.

bibliographic_review_management.lineage_overlap_notes: The paper positions itself against isolated small-satellite/CubeSat MBSE efforts and cites CubeSat reference-model and small-satellite design work; no previous extraction or corpus lineage file was read.

mbse_objective_scope_artifacts.stated_objective_pain_point: Satellite digital models are often mission-specific and isolated; reuse is cumbersome and error-prone, risking inconsistent traceability and functional misalignment. The paper proposes automated object-oriented functional modeling to generate reusable satellite platform functional architectures.
modeling_scope: New Space operational context and stakeholders at OA level
Satellite platform as primary system of interest
Capability/use-case groups such as Mission Goal, System Support, Safety, Reach Space, Zero Debris, Encryption, and Mission Phases
System Analysis and Logical Architecture functional elements, interfaces, and exchanges
Logical components, ports, and component exchanges
Functional libraries and automation scripts for model generation
mbse_objective_scope_artifacts.system_boundary_level_of_abstraction: The entire mission, company scope, and satellite platform are considered, but the satellite platform is selected as the SoI. Modeling spans operational context through logical/physical architecture, with solution-independent functional analysis before physical allocation.
mbse_objective_scope_artifacts.minimal_or_excluded_modeling: Detailed subsystem behavior, full mission linked models, explicit EPS design analysis, flight software/hardware implementation, and operational/flight validation are not reported; functional architecture is emphasized over behavioral simulation.
mbse_objective_scope_artifacts.required_prior_behavioral_domain_knowled: Users need stakeholder needs, mission objectives, standard platform baselines, use cases, established functional analyses/logical architectures, and discipline inputs such as power regulation/distribution concerns; detailed dynamic behavior is not required in the presented functional-library approach.
mbse_objective_scope_artifacts.handling_limited_behavioral_knowledge: Limited behavior knowledge is handled by abstract capability groupings, reusable functional groups, standardized baselines from previous missions, inheritance/encapsulation/polymorphism, and mission-specific extension of pre-defined functional libraries.

RQ1: A general small-satellite platform model can be organized around New Space stakeholders, mission objective domains, a satellite-platform SoI, and reusable capability groups across OA, SA, LA, and PA layers.
Limited behavioral detail is handled through abstract functional groups, standard functional libraries, pre-validated baselines, and object-oriented reuse rather than detailed subsystem simulation.

EPS is only represented adjacent to the system model through power-demanding components, Provide Power capability, PCDU links, power consumption criteria, and electrical regulation/distribution mapping examples.
RQ2: Claimed reproducibility outcomes include standardized digital replicability, reusable functional libraries, automated model generation, and consistent deployment across missions.

Claimed integrability outcomes include bidirectional data flow with Excel/JSON, external data/source connection through Python4Capella, and digital-thread handoff to physical architecture and discipline views.
Reliability is claimed mainly at the platform-standardization level, not demonstrated as an EPS or model-derived reliability improvement.
RQ3: The pilot integrates pre-physical validation at the model-structure level using manual inspection, functional-library interconnection checks, and Capella built-in model validation.
No EPS-specific verification artifacts, requirements, test cases, power-budget checks, or hardware integration tests are reported.
The paper states that automated functional verification mechanisms are future work.

author_stated_limitations_gaps: Initial modeling effort is higher during the transition to System as Code.
The custom automation layer across multiple APIs and Python classes requires disciplined management and has maintainability limitations.
Manual construction of functional libraries has scalability and maintainability limitations.
Capella's static nature limits interoperability, and Capella does not natively support code-model parallelism.
Capella element IDs are assigned only after model generation, so parameter mapping cannot be fully pre-defined.
Further work may integrate automated functional verification mechanisms.
extractor_identified_limitations_gaps: Pilot mission details, stakeholder evaluation, and quantitative metrics are absent.
No public Capella model, functional-library data, or Python scripts are reported.
EPS content is illustrative and adjacent, not a dedicated EPS model or verification case.
Venue details are not visible in the markdown front matter and are inferred from included IEEE/DOI metadata.
Reliability, cost, and schedule benefits are mostly asserted or conceptually motivated rather than empirically measured.

direct_evidence_quotes.quote: Even when based on standard methodologies, the reuse of model elements remains cumbersome and error-prone, leading to risks of inconsistent traceability and functional misalignment across missions.
For this research, the satellite platform was chosen as the primary SoI, aligning with the practical needs of the New Space industry while allowing future extension to broader system elements.

The objective of this structured capability mapping is to enhance modularity, support traceability between mission and system-level requirements, and facilitate the reuse of standard architectural elements within MBSE workflows.
Main Automation Script is used to deploy the automation program within Capella.

Further work may explore the integration of automated functional verification mechanisms to complement the structural and semantic validation demonstrated in this study
While Capella does not natively support code-model parallelism, the Python4Capella integration enabled structured automation and bidirectional data exchange
